title: How to Set Up a React + Vite Project in 2025 (The Right Way)
description: A complete, opinionated guide to scaffolding a React 19 + Vite project with TypeScript, routing, environment config, and deployment — avoiding the common setup mistakes.

author: MyAppAI Team

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Vite replaced Create React App as the default way to start a React project, and for good reason: instant dev server startup, fast hot module replacement, and a build based on Rollup that produces lean output. But the default scaffold leaves a lot of decisions unmade. This guide covers the setup that survives contact with a real project — TypeScript, routing, environment variables, linting, and deployment.

sections.heading: Scaffolding
sections.body:
You need Node.js 18 or newer. Scaffold with the official template:

```bash npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts cd my-app npm install npm run dev ```

The `react-ts` template gives you React 19 with TypeScript preconfigured. If you don't want TypeScript yet, use `react` — but for anything beyond a toy project, TypeScript pays for itself within the first week through editor autocompletion and catching prop-type mistakes before runtime.

Take a minute to look at what you got: `index.html` at the root (Vite processes it as the entry point, unlike CRA's public folder approach), `src/main.tsx` as the JS entry, and a `vite.config.ts` you'll extend as the project grows.

sections.heading: Project Structure That Scales
sections.body:
The default `src/` works for a demo. For a real app, organize by feature from the start — retrofitting structure later is painful:

``` src/ components/ # shared UI: Button, Modal, Spinner features/ # one folder per domain area auth/ dashboard/ hooks/ # shared custom hooks lib/ # API clients, formatting helpers pages/ # route-level components styles/ # global CSS, theme tokens ```

The rule: if two features need it, it goes in `components/` or `lib/`; otherwise it lives with its feature. This keeps imports short and makes features deletable without archaeology.

sections.heading: TypeScript Configuration Worth Setting
sections.body:
The template's `tsconfig` is reasonable, but two settings are worth verifying:

`"strict": true` — catches null/undefined errors at compile time. Leave it on. `"noUnusedLocals": true` and `"noUnusedParameters": true` — dead code gets flagged instead of accumulating.

Path aliases save you from `../../../../` import hell. In `tsconfig.json`:

```json { "compilerOptions": { "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } } } ```

And mirror it in `vite.config.ts` with the `resolve.alias` option so both the editor and the bundler agree.

sections.heading: Routing
sections.body:
Vite doesn't include a router. Install React Router:

```bash npm install react-router-dom ```

Set up your routes in one place so the app's navigation is auditable:

```tsx import { createBrowserRouter, RouterProvider } from 'react-router-dom'; import HomePage from './pages/HomePage'; import DashboardPage from './pages/DashboardPage';

const router = createBrowserRouter([ { path: '/', element: <HomePage /> }, { path: '/dashboard', element: <DashboardPage /> }, ]);

export default function App() { return <RouterProvider router={router} />; } ```

For static hosting (Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages), `createBrowserRouter` needs a SPA fallback configured on the host — otherwise refreshing on `/dashboard` returns a 404. Every major static host supports this with one setting or a small config file; set it up before you deploy, not after the first user reports it.

sections.heading: Environment Variables
sections.body:
Vite exposes variables prefixed with `VITE_` to client code via `import.meta.env`:

```bash

VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 ```

```ts const apiUrl = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL; ```

Three rules: never commit `.env` files with secrets (add them to `.gitignore`); remember that `VITE_` variables are embedded in the client bundle and therefore public — API keys that must stay secret belong on a backend; and use your host's dashboard for production values rather than committing a `.env.production`.

sections.heading: Linting and Formatting
sections.body: Install ESLint with the React and TypeScript configs, plus Prettier, and wire them to run on save in your editor and in a pre-commit hook. This sounds like ceremony, but inconsistent formatting in a team (or a solo project six months later) is a real drag on readability. The template includes an ESLint config — extend it rather than starting from zero.

sections.heading: Styling: Pick One Approach
sections.body:
Decision paralysis over styling kills momentum. The practical options:

Tailwind CSS — fastest for most projects; utility classes keep styling colocated with markup. The Vite plugin setup takes five minutes. CSS Modules — good if you prefer writing actual CSS with scoped class names. A component library (Mantine, Chakra, shadcn) — best when you need a full design system without a designer.

Pick one per project. Mixing Tailwind and CSS-in-JS and plain CSS in the same codebase is how stylesheets become unmaintainable.

sections.heading: State Management
sections.body: Start with React's built-in tools: `useState` and `useReducer` for local state, Context for genuinely global state like the authenticated user or theme. Reach for a library (Zustand is the current pragmatic favorite — tiny API, no boilerplate) when prop drilling gets painful or multiple distant components need the same data. For server state — data fetched from an API — use TanStack Query instead of hand-rolled `useEffect` fetching; it handles caching, refetching, and loading states better than you will.

sections.heading: Building and Deploying
sections.body:
```bash npm run build ```

This type-checks (if your build script includes `tsc`) and emits static files to `dist/`. Preview locally with `npm run preview` before deploying — it serves the production build, which occasionally behaves differently from dev mode.

Deployment is a solved problem: push to GitHub and connect the repo to Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, or Vercel. Set the build command to `npm run build`, the output directory to `dist`, and configure the SPA fallback mentioned above. Every push to your main branch deploys automatically.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
Skipping the SPA fallback and discovering client-side routing 404s in production. Putting secrets in `VITE_` variables and publishing your API keys to the world. No TypeScript strict mode, which forfeits the main benefit of using TypeScript. Fetching data in `useEffect` without cleanup, causing state updates on unmounted components and duplicate requests in StrictMode. Installing a state management library on day one for state that `useState` would have handled.

Get the scaffold right once, and every feature after it gets easier. Get it wrong, and you'll feel it in every file you touch.
